USMLE-style practice · Pharmacology

Early skin necrosis

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

Several days after starting warfarin without appropriate initial anticoagulant coverage, a patient with protein C deficiency develops painful purpuric plaques that become necrotic. Which mechanism best explains this early complication despite warfarin being prescribed as an anticoagulant?

  1. Early loss of protein C creates transient hypercoagulability
  2. Immediate depletion of all circulating platelets
  3. Direct chemical burning of subcutaneous tissue
  4. Excess activation of plasmin at dermal vessels
  5. Selective vitamin K accumulation in the skin
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Early loss of protein C creates transient hypercoagulability

Protein C can decline before longer-lived procoagulant factors, favoring microthrombosis.

Understanding the options

Early loss of protein C creates transient hypercoagulability
Protein C can decline before longer-lived procoagulant factors, favoring microthrombosis.
Immediate depletion of all circulating platelets
Warfarin does not typically cause immediate platelet depletion.
Direct chemical burning of subcutaneous tissue
The lesions are thrombotic rather than a local chemical burn.
Excess activation of plasmin at dermal vessels
Excess fibrinolysis does not explain thrombotic necrosis.
Selective vitamin K accumulation in the skin
Vitamin K accumulation is not the relevant mechanism.
